messages.subject: Lighthouse Example
parts:
Hey everyone,

I'm new to the bayesian estimation world but stumbled across a nice example that answers the following question:

A lighthouse is somewhere off a piece of straight coastline at a position α along the shore and a distance β out at sea. It emits a series of short highly collimated flashes at random intervals and hence at random azimuths. These pulses are intercepted on the coast by photo-detectors that record only the fact that a flash has occurred, but not the angle from which it came. N flashes have so far been recorded at positions {xk}. Where is the lighthouse?’ – Sivia, pg.29

 The example uses Stan to model this as the following:

model <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    real x_[N];
  }
 
  parameters {
    real alpha;
    real<lower=0> beta;
  }
 
  model {
    alpha ~ uniform(0, 20);
    beta  ~ uniform(0, 50);


    for (k in 1:N) {
      x_[k] ~ cauchy(alpha, beta);
    }    
  }
'

It's a simple example, however, I'm having trouble framing this problem in the brms formula format. I'd appreciate any advice on this.

Thanks!

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Lighthouse Example
parts:
sample_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100))

bform <- bf(x ~ 1, nu = 1)
fit <- brm(bform, data = sample_data, family = student())
summary(fit)

The 'nu = 1' fixes the degress of freedom of the student-t distribution to 1 so that we have a cauchy distribution.

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Lighthouse Example
parts:
So if anyone is ever curious. Here's my final solution in brms:

library(brms)

gen_data <- function(alpha, beta, n = 100){
  theta <- -pi / 2 + pi * runif(n)
  x <- alpha + beta * tan(theta)
  return(x)
}

sample_data <- data.frame(x = gen_data(10, 30, 100))


fit <- brm(
  bf(x ~ 1, nu = 1),
  data = sample_data,
  prior = c(
    set_prior("uniform(0, 20)", class = "Intercept"),
    set_prior("uniform(0, 50)", class = "sigma")
    ),
  family = student()
)

Where the Intercept here is alpha and sigma is beta of the Cauchy distribution from the example. There was a warning about supplying an upper bounded prior for sigma but the estimated values look good. Thanks Paul!
